newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Space monkey's death longshot misfortune - expert.
newsitem.headline: Space monkey's death longshot misfortune - expert.

text.p: The death of a monkey called Multik just returned to Earth from a two-week space flight, was a highly improbable and unfortunate accident, a leading scientist connected with the mission said on Friday.
"There is a very low mortality rate in these matters, one in 2,000," Inessa Kozlovskaya, a senior official at Moscow's Institute for Biomedical Problems, told a news conference.
"How is it that the one in 2,000 comes up when it matters most? Well, it's just Sod's law (bad luck)."

Multik, one of two male macaque monkeys aboard the craft, died of a heart attack on Wednesday after undergoing medical tests under general anaesthetic. Laptik, his flight partner alongside insects, snails and plants, suffered no ill effects.
"Multik suffered cardiac arrest just as the air tube was being pulled out and he began to cough," Kozlovskaya said. "We spent 50 minutes trying to revive him but we failed."
The U.S. space agency NASA put up half the cost of the $30 million mission, during which the monkeys' brains were wired up to electrodes as part of research into weightlessness.
Animal rights groups in the United States protested against the experiment, the latest in a research programme begun by the Soviet Union in 1973. The next Bion flight is due next year.

Scientists said the flight, intended to help understand the effects of weightlessness on humans, had been a huge success up to the incident on the operating table. Nearly all data had been recovered from the two monkeys, Kozlovskaya said.
"It was a high price to pay," she said. "We're grieving. We're in shock."
